newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Mercedes sees "A" class invading Golf terrain.
newsitem.headline: Mercedes sees "A" class invading Golf terrain.

text.p: BRUSSELS, June 10 - German luxury car maker Mercedes Benz said on Tuesday its new mini-car will take a big bite out of the sales of mass car maker Volkswagen AG's staple product, the Golf.

Jurgen Hubbert, head of Daimler-Benz Ag's Mercedes division told a conference organised by Automotive News Europe that the little "A" class to be launched in September promised great success for Mercedes and trouble for the competition.
"I'm happy (Volkswagen board chairman Ferdinand) Mr Piech has disappeared. We're in the Golf class here," Hubbert told a questioner who asked where would "A" class sales would come from.
Piech made a speech to the conference last night.
"Incoming orders (for the "A" class) are unbelievable. 500 people a day are ordering the car without having seen it or driven it. One third of these sales are coming from VW customers," Hubbert said.
Mercedes says that its first venture into the lower reaches of the market place has the interior space of a big family car like the Opel Vectra or Ford Mondeo in a body shorter than the tiny Ford Ka.

Mercedes has taken a big chance with the "A" class, a strange looking egg shaped car, analysts say. Mercedes has set tough sales targets for the "A" class and other new offerings, the even tinier Smart car made in a joint venture with Switzerland's SMH Ag, and a sport utility vehicle built in Alabama.
In a speech to the conference Hubbert said Mercedes planned to increase sales from around 650,000 in 1996, to 1.2 million by 2000.
One analyst said this implied that the "A" class quickly reached its production maximum of 200,000 a year, and that the Smart car and "M" class sport utility took off quickly.
Hubbert said Mercedes' traditional markets were not expected to increase much, so it was important for it to seek new sales niches. Mercedes would offer premium products in more sectors.
One questioner asked whether "A" class margins might be too thin.

"Every car project must have a 12 percent capital ratio, and I'm sure we can achieve this (with the "A" class)," Hubbert said. "We need cars like this going into new segments. This has good environment qualities and fuel consumption of four to six litres per 100 kilometres."
